boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Moorefield record (August 7, 1864) in Early's Raid and Operations Against the B&O Railroad [June-August 1864]. The August 4 attack on New Creek and the pursuit from Hancock are context. Campaign-wide marches, levies, captures, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Divisions; the live field reads zero. Johnson says his First and Second Maryland together had not 130 men in camp, and that McCausland's courier reported Averell passing Romney with three brigades of cavalry. Pond names Averell's brigades under Gibson and Powell and a battalion under Major Work.
claims.rationale: Fragmentary unit counts and reported enemy composition; no whole-force count for either side. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: Johnson says McCausland chose the camps: McCausland on the Moorefield side of the South Branch, Johnson's brigade along the Romney road for grass, his outer regiment four and a half miles from Moorefield. He calls his camp level ground with every artillery position favouring an attacker, the good hills being on McCausland's side of the river. Pond says the attack drove Johnson through the stream to the main position on the opposite bank.
claims.rationale: An interested subordinate's description and a history; the camps were chosen during the raid and are not tagged inherited.

claims.value: Johnson says McCausland commanded the expedition, chose camps, routes and pickets, slept in Moorefield three miles from his camp, and arrived after part of Johnson's brigade had crossed the river; he asks for a court of inquiry and alleges plunder weakened the fight. Pond credits Gibson's and Powell's brigades with the attack. The frozen commanders are Brigadier Generals John McCausland and William W. Averell.
claims.rationale: Johnson's charges are an interested subordinate's allegations against his superior, not an adjudication; neither listed commander receives automatic sole credit or blame.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Union victory and the live result Union Victory. Pond says the whole Confederate body was soon in disorderly retreat; Johnson says that after the river fight the enemy only followed him. NPS and Early (as quoted by Pond) say the defeat damaged the Confederate cavalry for the rest of the campaign.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. The later effect on the cavalry is campaign context, not the tactical result.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 531 total; the live field reads 531 (US 31; CS 500). Pond says Averell captured four guns, over 400 horses, three flags and 420 prisoners including 38 officers, with his own loss given as 41 killed and wounded. Johnson gives his brigade's net loss as about 300 missing (150 having come in) and the attackers' loss at the river as 2 majors and 38 men.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Kelley's figures in the Volume XLIII continuation were read but not selected.

open_questions: Averell's Moorefield report (Volume XLIII Part 1, p.493), Kelley's continuation (read, not selected), McCausland's report and Lee's dispatch remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. George E. Pond's The Shenandoah Valley in 1864 (Scribner, 1883) is a retrospective history written, by its preface, from the official documents at the War Records Office and field despatches; it quotes the reports of the commanders it describes and is not independent of them. Bradley T. Johnson's August 10, 1864 report, printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XLIII, Part 1, is one family of interested Confederate accounts; its July 28-August 3 portion in Volume XXXVII Part 1 was read but not selected. The Official Records volumes are shared containers, not additional witnesses. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
